title: Drifting like an infant
hookLine: others are busy and bright; I alone drift, like a baby not yet smiling (Tao Te Ching 20)

cards: The square is full. Music, lanterns, food going around on platters, people calling to each other across the crowd. Everyone has somewhere to be and something to say.
Off to one side, a single person stands still. Not sulking, not judging. Just not swept up.
Ask what they're doing, and the honest answer is nothing much. Chapter twenty of the Tao Te Ching is spoken by that person. It says I, and the I sounds a little lonely, and a little free.

teach.b: First, the crowd at the feast. The chapter describes the people around the speaker as bright and pleased, as if at a great banquet, or climbing a terrace in spring. Nothing in the text says they are wicked.
They are simply full, busy, sure of what they're doing.
Second, I alone, adrift. Against that brightness the speaker sets himself. Others have more than enough; he seems to have lost something.
Others are sharp and clear; he seems dull and murky, restless as the sea, blown about like a wind with nowhere to stop.
It reads like a confession of failure, and some readers think it's meant to sound that way, a little wry, a little sad.
Third, an infant not yet smiling. Then the picture at the center. In Legge's translation: "I am like an infant which has not yet smiled."
A newborn hasn't started performing. It hasn't learned to smile on cue, to look interested, to keep up. It just drifts, taking everything in.
The speaker has stayed, or gone back, to that early place, before the social face goes on.
The chapter ends by naming what sets the speaker apart: he values being fed by the mother. Some readers take the mother to be the Tao itself, the source this book keeps returning to.
So the drifting isn't aimless after all. It's a person who stopped grabbing at the banquet because they are already being fed.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter twenty as permission to do nothing for a while: a stretch of unscheduled time, with no goal, when they are not trying to keep up with anyone.

games.q: what does “drifting like an infant” mean?
o: acting childish to dodge grown-up responsibilities
resting apart from the crowd, unperformed, still fed
giving up and letting every duty slide

p: as if at a great banquet
what the speaker is fed by

s: chapter twenty says the crowd at the feast is wicked
the text calls them bright and pleased, not wicked. they're just swept up.
the speaker says he is like an infant that hasn't yet smiled
"I am like an infant which has not yet smiled," in Legge's translation.
the speaker boasts that he is the sharpest one in the crowd
he calls himself dull and murky, while the others are sharp and clear.

games.q: you're the speaker of chapter twenty. the whole crowd is feasting, bright and busy. what do you do?
o: join in and keep up with them.
stand apart, adrift, like a baby not yet smiling.
climb up and lecture them about simplicity.
games.why: he stays apart and drifts, unperformed. and he says why: he values being fed by the mother.

practice: Be unbusy for a moment: don't meditate, and don't improve anything. Let your face go slack, the way a face looks before anyone is watching, and let your eyes rest on whatever is in front of them without naming it.
If a task tugs at you, let it tug, and stay where you are, at the edge of the square.

wordCard.voice: Drifting like an infant. Chapter twenty's picture of someone not swept up by the crowd, unperformed, still being fed by the source. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, yīng'ér zhī wèi hái: an infant not yet smiling, from Tao Te Ching 20.

carryVoice: Your line: drifting. Under the ready smile and the busy look, there's a face that doesn't have to perform. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: I am like an infant which has not yet smiled.
